t: Number of Subarrays That Match a Pattern I
o: Convert each adjacent pair of `nums` into a comparison signature: +1 if increasing, 0 if equal, -1 if decreasing. A subarray of length m+1 starting at i matches `pattern` exactly when its m signatures equal `pattern[0..m-1]`. In example 2, signatures of `[1,4,4,1,3,5,5,3]` are [1,0,-1,1,1,0,-1], containing [1,0,-1] twice. With n, m ≤ 100, checking every start position against the pattern directly costs at most ~10,000 comparisons — brute force is fully sufficient.
k: Reduce nums to a signature array s[i] = sign(nums[i+1] - nums[i]).
The answer is the number of occurrences of pattern as a contiguous substring of s.
Tiny constraints make O(n·m) matching perfectly fine; string-matching algorithms are overkill.

a.i: Precompute the comparison signs once, then slide a window of width m over the signature array and compare element-wise. This avoids repeated comparisons of raw values and makes the code a simple double loop.
s: Build s of length n-1 where s[i] encodes the relation between nums[i] and nums[i+1].
For each start i from 0 to n-1-m, check s[i..i+m-1] == pattern.
a.t: O(n·m) — for each of O(n) windows we compare up to m signs; with n,m ≤ 100 this is trivial.

w: Use this direct scan in an interview; mention KMP/Z-algorithm or rolling hash as the scalable follow-up if n were 10^5+. Pitfalls: off-by-one on window count (there are n-m windows of length m+1) and mishandling the equality sign (0). Edge cases: all-equal runs and patterns of all 0s.
